cards.front: A well child has small, firm, shiny skin-coloured papules with central umbilication. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context: This poxvirus infection spreads through direct skin contact and autoinoculation. Lesions usually clear spontaneously, although this can take many months.

cards.front: Amblyopia = reduced vision from abnormal visual development; critical treatment period is before age 7-8; treat with patching of the [___] eye.
cards.context:
Amblyopia (reduced vision in one eye despite structurally normal eye) develops when one eye's input is suppressed during the critical period of visual development.

Critical period for treatment is before age 7-8 — after this, visual pathways become much less plastic and improvement is limited.

Treat with patching of the better eye.

cards.front: An obese 10-year-old still snores with witnessed apnoeas after adenotonsillectomy. Treat this as [___] OSA and reassess severity with polysomnography rather than assuming surgery cured it.
cards.context:
Adenotonsillectomy treats the common adenotonsillar obstruction but is not a cure guarantee. Obesity, severe baseline OSA and craniofacial, genetic or neuromuscular comorbidity make residual disease more likely.

Ongoing snoring or witnessed pauses after surgery should trigger objective reassessment with polysomnography rather than another recall of the original first-line rule.

A sleep or ENT team then targets any remaining obstruction; CPAP is an option when clinically significant OSA persists without a suitable site-specific treatment.

cards.front: A child with an abdominal mass develops leg weakness and new urinary retention. The imaging study to assess the spinal canal is [___].
cards.context:
Weakness, altered gait or bladder symptoms in a child with a possible neuroblastoma suggest pressure on the spinal cord. This is a neurological emergency rather than a routine abdominal-mass work-up.

MRI is the modality that shows intraspinal extension and cord compromise. Arrange urgent specialist assessment while maintaining neurological observations.

cards.front: Endotracheal tube size in a child over 1 year: cuffed internal diameter = age/4 + [___], inserted to a lip depth of age/2 + 12 cm.
cards.context:
The formulas are for children over 1 year: uncuffed internal diameter = age/4 + 4; cuffed = age/4 + 3.5. Cuffed tubes are now standard in most Australian paediatric practice outside the newborn.

Depth at the lip is age/2 + 12 cm for oral tubes. Always have a tube one size up and one size down drawn ready.

The cross-check after intubation is the same as ever: symmetrical chest rise, misting, waveform capnography, and equal air entry.

cards.front: Osmotic diarrhoea stops on fasting; secretory diarrhoea [___] on fasting.
cards.context:
The fasting test is the bedside discriminator.

Osmotic diarrhoea is driven by unabsorbed solutes (lactose in lactase deficiency, sorbitol from chewing gum) drawing water into the lumen — remove the trigger and diarrhoea stops within 24-48 h.

cards.front: When bile flow is obstructed (cholestasis) in a child, the two LFT enzymes that rise are ALP and [___], rather than the hepatocellular ALT/AST.
cards.context:
ALP and GGT mark the bile-duct (cholestatic) side of the panel and climb when bile can't drain (e.g. biliary atresia in a jaundiced infant).

The trap in paediatrics: ALP also rises from growing bone, so a high ALP is only cholestatic if GGT rises alongside it; isolated high ALP in a well child is often normal growth.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive mutation in the CFTR gene; most common mutation is [___] (~70% of alleles).
cards.context:
Recessive inheritance means a child needs two faulty CFTR alleles (one from each carrier parent) to be affected — which is why CF is autosomal recessive and unaffected siblings can still be carriers.

F508del is a three-base deletion losing phenylalanine at position 508. The misfolded protein is degraded before reaching the cell surface.

It dominates the mutation pool and defines which CFTR modulators a patient can use.

cards.front: Before choosing an allergy alternative, document the reaction's phenotype, [___], severity and subsequent beta-lactam tolerance.
cards.context:
Before replacing a beta-lactam, document the reaction, timing, severity and later tolerance of related drugs. RCH separates non-severe hypersensitivity from immediate or severe reactions.

A vague family label is not proven anaphylaxis. A convincing immediate or severe delayed reaction needs an appropriate alternative and, when needed, specialist advice.

cards.front: Early nutritional growth faltering may reduce weight while initially preserving length and [___] circumference.
cards.context: Prolonged or severe undernutrition can eventually affect all three measurements. Preserved head growth does not exclude inadequate nutrition.

cards.front: A comfortable baby who effortlessly brings up small amounts of milk after feeds while growing normally has physiological [___], from an immature lower oesophageal sphincter.
cards.context:
The 'happy spitter' has three reassuring legs: effortless spills, a comfortable baby, and normal growth. All three present means no tests and no drugs.

It fades by about 12 months as lower oesophageal sphincter tone builds. Lose any leg — distress, faltering growth, respiratory signs — and reframe it as GORD.

cards.front: In children, cardiac arrest (IV/IO) and anaphylaxis (IM) use the same weight-based adrenaline dose of [___] microg/kg — the route, concentration and maximum dose differ.
cards.context:
The two preparations exist for volume reasons. IM injection needs a small volume, so anaphylaxis uses the concentrated 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) — a thigh dose is roughly 0.1-0.5 mL.

An IV arrest dose from that same ampoule would be a fifth of a millilitre in a 20 kg child — hard to measure under pressure. Diluting to 1:10,000 makes the identical dose a drawable 2 mL.

Each strength is right for its route. The hazard is the interface: two ampoules, one drug name, a 10-fold gap, both on the trolley. That is why the request must always name the concentration.

cards.front: Asthma first aid is 4 puffs, 4 breaths each, then wait [___] before repeating.
cards.context:
The National Asthma Council 4 x 4 x 4 plan is what a coach, teacher or parent performs, and it is worth being able to recite. Sit the person upright.

 Give 4 separate puffs of salbutamol, one at a time through a spacer, taking 4 breaths from the spacer after each puff. Wait 4 minutes. If no improvement, give 4 more.

If there is still no improvement, call 000 and say 'severe asthma attack', then keep giving 4 puffs every 4 minutes until the ambulance arrives.

cards.front: Rolling tummy-to-back, reaching for a wanted toy, mouthing objects and leaning on the hands in sitting fit the NSW [___]-month profile.
cards.context:
NSW's six-month cluster combines rolling tummy-to-back, reaching for a wanted toy, mouthing objects and leaning on the hands while sitting.

It does not make fully unsupported sitting a hard six-month requirement. RCH instead treats inability to sit unsupported beyond nine months as a referral feature.

cards.front: A contaminated intra-abdominal or intracranial-abscess source often needs explicit [___] cover, commonly with metronidazole.
cards.context:
Anaerobic cover is driven by anatomy and source: oral or dental infection, intracranial abscess and intra-abdominal contamination are typical clues.

Metronidazole is often paired with an agent covering aerobic Gram-negative and streptococcal organisms; it is not a stand-alone answer for undifferentiated sepsis.

cards.front: Nephritic syndrome features: [___] (often cola-coloured), hypertension, and mild-moderate proteinuria; commonest paediatric cause is PSGN.
cards.context:
Nephritic syndrome reflects glomerular INFLAMMATION (contrast nephrotic = podocyte leak).

Inflamed glomeruli let red cells through, so haematuria with RBC casts is the hallmark, and proteinuria stays mild-to-moderate rather than nephrotic-range.

Falling GFR causes salt and water retention, which drives the hypertension and oedema. Cola/tea-coloured urine reflects RBC breakdown in acidic urine.

cards.front: Perthes (idiopathic femoral-head AVN) clusters in boys aged roughly [___] years; younger onset leaves more remodelling time.
cards.context:
Perthes is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in primary-school-age boys. SUFE typically affects overweight adolescents around the growth spurt.

Younger Perthes onset leaves more growth for femoral-head remodelling. Young children are often managed with containment and observation; older children more often need surgery.

Hip pain may be referred to the knee, so examine both. Fever with refusal to weight-bear raises concern for septic arthritis at any age.

cards.front: Pertussis presents with paroxysmal cough + inspiratory '[___]' + post-tussive vomiting; treat with azithromycin; infants <6 months may present with apnoea instead.
cards.context:
Pertussis classically has three stages: catarrhal (days 1-14, URTI-like — most contagious), paroxysmal (weeks 2-6, fits with inspiratory 'whoop', post-tussive vomiting, exhaustion), convalescent (weeks 6-10).

Infants <6 months may NOT whoop — present with apnoea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty (mortality ~1 in 125).

Vaccinated individuals can still transmit — hence adult/adolescent boosters + cocoon strategy.

cards.front: Atopic dermatitis affects 10-20% of children, with 85% of childhood cases beginning before age [___]. It can precede food allergy, allergic rhinitis and asthma, but this is an increased-risk association rather than a fixed progression.
cards.context:
Eczema affects 10-20% of children; about 85% of childhood cases begin before age 5. It reflects skin-barrier dysfunction and a Th2-skewed immune response.

Early or severe eczema is associated with later food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis. The 'atopic march' is a population association, not a fixed sequence; most children do not develop every condition.

cards.front: The classic triad of infectious mononucleosis is fever, [___], and lymphadenopathy.
cards.context:
The classic triad probes joint involvement of fever, the oropharynx (exudative pharyngitis), and lymphoid tissue (cervical lymphadenopathy, often with splenomegaly).

Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is more specific for EBV than anterior cervical adenopathy alone — the latter is just as common in bacterial pharyngitis.

cards.front: A small-for-dates newborn with congenital CMV is jaundiced, has hepatosplenomegaly and is covered in raised blue-purple papules of dermal haematopoiesis. This appearance is called a [___] rash.
cards.context:
Each papule is an island of extramedullary haematopoiesis in the dermis: 2 to 8 mm, bluish-red to purple, and palpable above the skin.

Rubella gave the classic description, but where rubella is vaccinated away congenital CMV is the likelier cause; toxoplasmosis, varicella and HIV can do the same.

Infection is not the only cause: neuroblastoma and leukaemia can seed the skin with similar dark nodules.

cards.front: Tap water is a poor storage medium for an avulsed permanent tooth because it is [___] and damages periodontal-ligament cells, but it is preferable to air-drying.
cards.context:
Successful replantation depends on keeping periodontal-ligament cells alive. Milk, HBSS, saline and the buccal sulcus are preferred; hypotonic tap water damages the cells.

If no preferred medium is available, water is still better than leaving the tooth to dry in air.

cards.front: Scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue from GABHS) is treated with [___].
cards.context:
Scarlet fever is GABHS (group A strep) pharyngitis plus an erythrogenic exotoxin rash.

The reason to actually give the antibiotic — even though the rash itself is self-limiting — is to prevent acute rheumatic fever (antibiotics do not prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

cards.front: In sickle cell disease, an acute focal neurological deficit requires immediate [___] without waiting for imaging.
cards.context:
Acute stroke is a major sickle cell disease complication. Start emergency transfusion with haematology immediately; do not wait for imaging, and aim to begin within 2 hours.

Exchange transfusion is preferred. If exchange cannot start within 2 hours and haemoglobin is ≤85 g/L, give a simple transfusion while exchange is arranged.

MRI/MRA is preferred. If unavailable without delay, use non-contrast CT to exclude haemorrhage and follow the paediatric stroke pathway. Annual transcranial Doppler from age 2 supports primary prevention.

cards.front: Global developmental delay workup: chromosomal [___], fragile X testing, thyroid function, metabolic screen; brain MRI if neurological signs.
cards.context:
Global developmental delay is delay in two or more domains. Start with chromosomal microarray, a separate Fragile X assay, thyroid function and history-directed metabolic testing.

Test hearing and vision in every child. Reserve brain MRI and neurology review for focal signs, dysmorphism, abnormal head size or regression.

Refer to a child-development service or general paediatrician, and begin early intervention while investigations proceed.

cards.front: Pancreatic insufficiency affects ~[___]% of CF patients, causing steatorrhoea; treat with PERT (Creon) with every meal/snack.
cards.context:
Pancreatic exocrine ducts plug with thick secretions → progressive acinar fibrosis → reduced enzyme delivery to gut → fat and protein malabsorption.

PERT (Creon) provides exogenous pancreatic enzymes: lipase, protease and amylase. Adjust dose to symptoms.

cards.front: An infant film shows a wide upper mediastinum. Two features argue it is a normal thymus rather than a mass: pulmonary [___] are still visible through it, and it does not compress the airway.
cards.context:
The commonest paediatric film error is calling a normal thymus pathological, and two negative features settle it.

A normal thymus is not very radio-opaque, so pulmonary vessels remain visible through it, and it never compresses the airway or adjacent vessels. A mediastinal mass does both.

Size alone is unreliable, because the thymus involutes during acute illness and rebounds afterwards.

cards.front: A previously aligned child develops sudden strabismus with headache and vomiting. The appropriate pathway is [___].
cards.context:
A new neurological squint is different from a stable childhood refractive squint. Sudden onset, diplopia, headache, vomiting or abnormal eye movements raises concern for an acquired neurological cause.

The RCH referral guidance places neurological strabismus in the urgent group. Escalate rather than arranging routine optometry review alone.

cards.front: In anaphylaxis the auto-injector can be given through [___] if undressing would delay the dose.
cards.context:
Intramuscular adrenaline is time-critical, so removing clothing must not delay treatment.

Press the auto-injector firmly against the outer mid-thigh (vastus lateralis); it can be given through clothing if needed, avoiding bulky seams or pocket contents.

Call emergency services and repeat the dose after 5 minutes if anaphylaxis persists, following the device instructions and ASCIA action plan.

cards.front: Modern paediatric airway measurements place the narrowest transverse dimension at the glottic opening rather than the cricoid ring; large [___] flexes the head when supine — counter with a shoulder roll.
cards.context:
Direct airway imaging and bronchoscopy show that the paediatric larynx is closer to cylindrical than the traditional funnel model; in measured transverse dimensions, the glottic opening is narrower than the cricoid ring.

Properly sized cuffed ETTs are acceptable when cuff pressure is monitored.

Large tongue + large occiput position the head in flexion when supine; place a small shoulder roll to neutralise the airway for intubation, not the head extension you'd use in an adult.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal [___] mutation in the CFTR gene; most common mutation is F508del (~70% of alleles).
cards.context:
Recessive inheritance means a child needs two faulty CFTR alleles (one from each carrier parent) to be affected — which is why CF is autosomal recessive and unaffected siblings can still be carriers.

F508del is a three-base deletion losing phenylalanine at position 508. The misfolded protein is degraded before reaching the cell surface.

It dominates the mutation pool and defines which CFTR modulators a patient can use.

cards.front: A child with scarlet fever should receive a 10-day course of oral [___] to eradicate Group A Streptococcus.
cards.context: Scarlet fever is toxin-mediated Group A streptococcal pharyngitis. A complete 10-day penicillin course eradicates the organism and reduces the risk of acute rheumatic fever.

cards.front: [___] (intramural bowel gas) on AXR is the hallmark radiological finding of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) in preterm neonates.
cards.context:
Ischaemic injury to the bowel mucosa allows gas-producing bacteria to enter the bowel wall, where the gas dissects between layers and shows up on AXR as linear or bubbly lucencies hugging the bowel contour.

Progression markers: portal venous gas (branching lucencies overlying the liver) indicates severe systemic dissemination, and free intraperitoneal air signals perforation requiring urgent surgery.

cards.front: Lower limit of systolic BP in children 1-10 years = 70 + ([___] × age); below this is hypotension and signals late-stage decompensated shock.
cards.context:
70 + (2 × age) gives the lower SBP limit in children 1-10 — a 5-year-old's floor is 80 mmHg. Useful in resus when age-specific tables aren't to hand.

The trap: children compensate via tachycardia and vasoconstriction up to ~30-40% volume loss, then crash. Hypotension means late Class III-IV shock (peri-arrest).

Treat tachycardia, cold peripheries, prolonged cap refill, oliguria, or altered mental status as compensated shock — don't wait for the BP to drop.

cards.front: A newborn develops abdominal distension and blood-stained stools. Necrotising enterocolitis rises higher on the differential if the birth history confirms [___] delivery.
cards.context:
An immature intestine is more vulnerable to the inflammation and tissue injury of this condition. Prematurity raises suspicion when an infant develops abdominal distension or bloody stools.

The illness can progress to bowel necrosis and perforation; these signs need urgent neonatal assessment.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis (CF) management pillars: airway clearance, dornase alfa, nebulised hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and pancreatic [___] replacement.
cards.context:
The five pillars of CF maintenance work together: daily airway clearance — positive expiratory pressure (PEP), active cycle of breathing (ACBT), exercise — prevents mucus stagnation.

Dornase alfa cleaves neutrophil DNA. Antibiotics: empirical for exacerbations, chronic suppressive (inhaled tobramycin for Pseudomonas); pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) for nutrition.

cards.front: Crohn's disease affects [___] to anus with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; small bowel Crohn's may present insidiously with growth failure.
cards.context:
Crohn's disease can affect anywhere from mouth to anus, with skip lesions (unaffected bowel between affected segments) and transmural inflammation that drives fistulas, strictures, and abscesses.

Small bowel Crohn's is insidious — vague abdominal pain, intermittent loose stool, growth failure, low-grade fevers — easily missed for months.

cards.front: Respiratory rate falls steadily with age: roughly [___] breaths/min for a term newborn, but only 14-25 breaths/min for an adolescent.
cards.context:
Respiratory rate is the vital sign that changes most across childhood, and it is also the one most often recorded badly — counted over ten seconds, or while the child is crying.

Count for a full minute in a settled child. A rate at the top of the range in a quiet, afebrile child is a genuine finding, not a rounding error.

The trap is anchoring to the adult 12-20: a rate of 40 is unremarkable in a newborn and alarming in a ten-year-old.

cards.front: An adolescent with exudative tonsillitis and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy likely has infectious [___].
cards.context:
EBV glandular fever in adolescents classically shows exudative pharyngitis with tender posterior cervical nodes — more specific than anterior nodes alone.

Splenomegaly carries contact-sport restriction because of rupture risk.

cards.front: The most damaging consequence of chronic otitis media in early childhood is [___] loss during the period of language acquisition.
cards.context: Early conductive hearing loss disrupts language acquisition, delaying speech and schooling. Persistent middle-ear disease is therefore urgent, not a nuisance.

cards.front: Most congenital diaphragmatic hernias are [___]-sided and herniate posterolaterally through the foramen of Bochdalek.
cards.context:
Side and site are both examinable, and they are not independent — the common defect is posterolateral and on the left.

Roughly 70 to 90 per cent are left-sided. A right-sided hernia is much harder to see because the liver plugs the defect and bowel is not a prominent feature, so presentation is often delayed.

cards.front: Avulsed primary (baby) teeth should NOT be replanted — risks damage to the developing successor tooth bud. Avulsed permanent teeth should be replanted within [___] minutes; if delayed, store in milk (or saline / buccal sulcus) to preserve the periodontal ligament.
cards.context:
Replantation rule splits by tooth type. PERMANENT: replant within 60 min (ideally <15 min); handle by crown only, rinse gently (preserves periodontal ligament), store in milk or saline if can't replant immediately.

PRIMARY (baby): do NOT replant — risks damaging the developing permanent tooth bud (ankylosis, infection, developmental disturbance).

Practical: adult/older child permanent tooth → milk, dentist within 30-60 min; toddler baby tooth → don't replant, dentist to assess remaining teeth and soft tissue (permanent teeth erupt age 6+).

cards.front: Otoscopy pinna technique: pull up-and-back in adults and older children; pull [___]-and-back in infants. The infant ear canal is soft and angled differently — adult technique collapses it and you'll see canal wall, not the tympanic membrane.
cards.context:
Pinna manipulation straightens the external auditory canal for line-of-sight to the tympanic membrane.

Wrong technique = looking at canal wall, not the membrane. The infant trap is that adult technique collapses the soft canal.

Use the smallest speculum, brace hand on the child's head, brief glance is enough.

cards.front: In anaphylaxis, repeat the IM adrenaline dose every [___] if there is no improvement.
cards.context: If the first IM adrenaline dose has not worked, the answer is another dose — not a switch to antihistamines or steroids. Reassess airway, breathing and circulation between doses.

cards.front: Pertussis presents with paroxysmal cough + inspiratory 'whoop' + post-tussive vomiting; treat with [___]; infants <6 months may present with apnoea instead.
cards.context:
Pertussis classically has three stages: catarrhal (days 1-14, URTI-like — most contagious), paroxysmal (weeks 2-6, fits with inspiratory 'whoop', post-tussive vomiting, exhaustion), convalescent (weeks 6-10).

Infants <6 months may NOT whoop — present with apnoea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty (mortality ~1 in 125).

Vaccinated individuals can still transmit — hence adult/adolescent boosters + cocoon strategy.

cards.front: The mainstay of bronchiolitis management is [___] care.
cards.context: The hard part is doing less. Bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics don't change the course — care is feeding support, oxygen when SpO2 is persistently below the PREDICT age/risk threshold (see below), and time.

cards.front: Night terrors arise from a partial arousal out of deep slow-wave sleep, which is sleep stage [___].
cards.context:
Night terrors are a partial arousal out of deep slow-wave sleep, which is why the child is inconsolable and has no memory of the event afterwards.

Because slow-wave sleep is concentrated early, they cluster in the first third of the night.

cards.front: An overweight adolescent with hip or knee pain and an externally rotated leg has [___].
cards.context: The adolescent end of the spectrum, and a surgical emergency. The femoral head slips off the neck through the growth plate; classically an overweight peripubescent boy, and knee pain is a red herring.

cards.front: A 5-year-old with buttock purpura develops colicky pain and a sausage-shaped mass. Unlike infantile intussusception, HSP intussusception is typically [___] and can be missed on the usual ultrasound window.
cards.context: Infantile intussusception is ileocolic. HSP intussusception is ileo-ileal, so the usual right-iliac-fossa ultrasound window can miss it. The vignette is unanswerable from 'HSP plus abdominal pain' alone.

cards.front: Constipation: most common GI complaint in paediatrics; over [___]% is functional (no organic cause).
cards.context:
Constipation accounts for 3-5% of all paediatric outpatient visits — the commonest GI presentation.

The remaining 5% have organic causes (Hirschsprung, hypothyroid, spinal cord, neuromuscular) — flag with red-flag features.

cards.front: Genetic testing for the common 5q form of spinal muscular atrophy looks for disease-causing changes in both copies of [___].
cards.context:
The primary injury is to anterior horn motor neurons, even though weakness and wasting are visible in the muscles.

The related SMN2 gene can modify severity by supplying some functional protein; it is not the usual disease-causing gene being tested here.

cards.front: First-line treatment for paediatric OSA caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy is [___].
cards.context:
Paediatric OSA is mostly an anatomic problem — adenotonsillar tissue crowding the oropharyngeal airway during sleep.

Untreated paediatric OSA is not a benign sleep complaint: it drives growth failure, behavioural and learning problems often misdiagnosed as ADHD, and in severe cases right-heart strain.

cards.front: Sudden high fever and soft stridor in an unimmunised child who refuses to lie flat and has no barking cough: suspect [___] and keep the child calm and upright.
cards.context:
Immunisation status is the modern clue: Hib disease now appears almost exclusively in unvaccinated or partially vaccinated children, so an unimmunised child shifts the odds sharply.

Posture is protective — lying flat lets the swollen supraglottis fall back over the laryngeal inlet, so let the child stay upright on a parent's lap while senior airway help is mobilised.

cards.front: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) F:M ratio is [___]:1 — the only hip condition with female preponderance; incidence ~4 in 1000 live births.
cards.context:
DDH is a spectrum from subluxable through dislocatable to fully dislocated. Incidence ~4 in 1000 live births, F:M ratio 6:1 — the only hip condition with strong female predominance (maternal hormone ligamentous laxity).

Risk factors (5 Fs): Female, Firstborn, Family history, Feet down (breech), Fluid low (oligohydramnios). Routine screening at birth + 6-week check.

cards.front: A boy's foreskin remains trapped behind the swollen glans despite analgesia, compression and gentle reduction attempts in ED. The doctor keeps him fasted and requests urgent [___] review.
cards.context:
The trapped foreskin obstructs venous drainage, worsening oedema and making reduction harder. Continued constriction can threaten tissue perfusion.

Analgesia, compression and gentle reduction usually work. If reduction fails, keep the child fasted and obtain urgent paediatric surgical review; repeated forceful attempts risk further injury.

A dusky or dark glans requires urgent surgical review from the outset. Successful reduction in a child who can pass urine usually permits discharge with advice to prevent recurrence.

cards.front: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) increases future suicide risk by [___]×; never dismiss 'superficial' injuries — assess lethality, intent, and underlying psychiatric distress.
cards.context:
NSSI is usually emotion regulation or communication, not intent to die — but it overlaps with suicide. NSSI raises future suicide attempt risk 4-7×, so 'superficial cutting for attention' should never be dismissed.

Assess function, method/lethality (depth, location, dose), intent at the time, current intent, and access to means.

cards.front: In cystic fibrosis, obstruction of small airways by viscous secretions causes bronchial wall damage and bronchiectasis, typically worst in the [___] lobes.
cards.context:
The structural lung damage of cystic fibrosis has a lobar preference worth knowing.

Viscous secretions obstruct small airways, causing distal atelectasis and progressive bronchial wall damage. The resulting bronchiectasis is typically worst in the upper lobes.

cards.front: A 2-year-old on oral antibiotics for acute otitis media has worsening pain, fever and swelling behind the ear that displaces the pinna down and [___]. This is mastoiditis, which needs IV antibiotics rather than continued oral therapy.
cards.context:
Mastoiditis is the complication you are being asked to spot before it becomes intracranial, and the discriminator is where the swelling sits and what it does to the pinna.

Swelling is postero-superior to the pinna and pushes it down and forward — an appearance uncomplicated acute otitis media never produces. Progressive pain and fever despite antibiotics is the other clue.

It is mostly under 3 years, usually Strep pneumoniae, and late presentation risks meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and brain abscess.

cards.front: Two healthcare rescuers doing paediatric CPR use a ratio of [___], compressing one-third of chest depth at 100-120/min.
cards.context:
Healthcare-rescuer paediatric ratio is 15:2, not the adult 30:2. Depth one-third of the chest, rate 100-120.

Infant: two thumbs, hands encircling. Small child: heel of one hand.

cards.front: The most common cause of bronchiolitis in infants is [___].
cards.context:
Bronchiolitis is a winter epidemic in under-2s, and respiratory syncytial virus dominates the aetiology — about 70% of admissions, with rhinovirus, parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus making up most of the rest.

The reason to confirm RSV is mainly prognostic and infection-control: ex-prem infants and those with congenital heart disease have a much higher risk of severe disease.

cards.front: The strongest known genetic risk factor for atopic eczema is a loss-of-function mutation in the [___] gene, which encodes a structural barrier protein of the stratum corneum.
cards.context:
Links the mainstay to the pathophysiology: the commonest inherited lesion in eczema disrupts a key structural protein of the stratum corneum, so the skin cannot hold moisture.

This is why barrier-restoration (emollients) targets the root defect, not just the symptoms — and why these children are also prone to other atopic disease.

cards.front: Once cultures identify a susceptible pathogen, change broad empiric therapy to the [___] effective antibiotic and reassess dose for gestation and organ function.
cards.context:
Empiric cover is chosen for age, source, acquisition setting and resistance risk.

Once organism and susceptibilities are known, switch to the narrowest effective agent and set duration by the infected site and complications.

Neonatal gestation and renal or hepatic function can alter dosing and interval, so use a neonatal formulary and local antimicrobial service rather than memorising an adult schedule.

cards.front: Precocious puberty means secondary sexual characteristics before [___] of age in girls (or 9 years in boys).
cards.context: Name the age cut-offs first: before 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Central (gonadotrophin-dependent) is usually idiopathic in girls but warrants brain imaging in boys to exclude a CNS lesion.

cards.front: Epigastric pain, early satiety and postprandial fullness for months, with no organic cause and no alarm features (weight loss, vomiting, bleeding), is [___] dyspepsia.
cards.context:
Functional dyspepsia is a POSITIVE clinical diagnosis, not just 'all the tests were normal': epigastric pain or discomfort, early satiety, or postprandial fullness with no organic cause.

Rome IV asks for symptoms on at least 4 days/month for 2+ months. Alarm features that argue against it and force work-up: weight loss, vomiting, dysphagia, GI bleeding, nocturnal symptoms.

cards.front: Nebulised hypertonic saline (~6-7%) is used in CF to rehydrate airway surface liquid; pre-treat with [___] to prevent reflex bronchoconstriction.
cards.context:
Hypertonic saline (6-7%) draws water into the airway lumen by osmosis, rehydrating the surface liquid that CFTR dysfunction has dehydrated.

Pre-treat with a bronchodilator — the osmotic load can trigger reflex bronchoconstriction.

cards.front: An avulsed permanent tooth should be held only by the [___], and the root must never be scrubbed.
cards.context:
The root surface carries the periodontal ligament cells that decide whether the tooth reattaches. Fingers on the root, or scrubbing dirt off it, strip exactly the layer replantation depends on.

So the instruction is deliberately specific: pick it up by the crown, rinse gently under milk or saline if visibly dirty, and do not wipe, scrub or dry it.

cards.front: Central precocious puberty in girls is idiopathic in >90% of cases, but in boys an underlying CNS pathology (hypothalamic [___], tumour, hydrocephalus) is present in ~75% — so MRI brain is mandatory in every male.
cards.context:
Central precocious puberty (CPP) is early HPG-axis activation — normal pubertal sequence and progression, but starting too early (girls <8 years, boys <9 years). In girls, >90% is idiopathic.

In boys, 75% have an underlying CNS lesion (hypothalamic hamartoma, tumour, hydrocephalus) — much higher index of suspicion needed. MRI brain is mandatory in boys with CPP.

cards.front: Infantile haemangioma: most common benign soft tissue tumour; 3 phases — proliferative ([___] months), plateau, involution (50% by age 5); first-line treatment is oral propranolol.
cards.context:
Infantile haemangiomas are the commonest benign soft tissue tumour of childhood — not usually present at birth, appear in first weeks.

Most need no treatment.

Treat (oral propranolol first-line) for: ulceration, periorbital (amblyopia risk), nasal tip (anatomic distortion), large, multiple, or symptomatic.

cards.front: The classic triad of infectious mononucleosis is fever, pharyngitis, and [___].
cards.context:
The classic triad probes joint involvement of fever, the oropharynx (exudative pharyngitis), and lymphoid tissue (cervical lymphadenopathy, often with splenomegaly).

Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is more specific for EBV than anterior cervical adenopathy alone — the latter is just as common in bacterial pharyngitis.

cards.front: A 3-year-old with viral gastroenteritis keeps vomiting and is failing oral rehydration. The single-dose oral antiemetic shown to reduce vomiting and the need for IV fluids is [___].
cards.context:
This antiemetic roughly halves persistent vomiting and cuts IV-fluid and admission need in mild-to-moderate gastroenteritis when given as a single oral wafer before restarting small-volume oral rehydration.

Avoid in infants under 6 months and where the QT interval may be prolonged.

cards.front: In an injured child, which routine vital sign can remain deceptively normal despite significant haemorrhage? [___]
cards.context: Compensated shock masks substantial blood loss. Blood pressure may stay normal until late, so use tachycardia, cool peripheries and prolonged capillary refill to detect shock earlier.

cards.front: When pyloric stenosis remains clinically suspected after an equivocal scan, the next imaging step is [___].
cards.context:
Early pyloric stenosis can lack a palpable olive or metabolic alkalosis.

An equivocal initial scan does not exclude it when progressively forceful, non-bilious vomiting continues.

cards.front: Newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) tests for [___], which are absent when thymic T-cell production fails.
cards.context:
T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are DNA loops made during thymic T-cell maturation. Low or absent TRECs on the newborn bloodspot means poor thymic output.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is treatable if found before Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) or disseminated Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG).

reference.title: ASCIA-TAPID Consensus Guideline: Diagnosis, Management and Transplantation of SCID in Australia and New Zealand

cards.front: The ONLY first-line life-saving treatment in anaphylaxis is IM [___] to the mid-outer thigh.
cards.context:
Adrenaline reverses anaphylaxis on multiple fronts: α1 vasoconstriction restores BP, β1 supports CO, β2 bronchodilates + stabilises mast cells.

Give 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM into the mid-outer thigh (vastus lateralis); the deltoid is too thin (slower absorption).

cards.front: A febrile infant aged [___] days or younger needs full evaluation + admission for empirical IV antibiotics even if well-appearing.
cards.context:
Any infant aged 28 days or younger by corrected age with fever ≥38°C or hypothermia <36°C needs admission, a serious-bacterial-infection workup and prompt empirical IV antibiotics, even if well.

Obtain blood culture, catheter/SPA urine and, unless contraindicated, CSF. Appearance is unreliable because neonates may not localise or contain infection.

RCH empiric therapy: ≤48 hours after birth, benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; >48 hours without meningitis, cefazolin plus gentamicin. Suspected meningitis needs benzylpenicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin.

cards.front: Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability; detected by raised [___] on newborn screen; start levothyroxine ideally within 2 weeks.
cards.context:
Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability — affects 1 in 3000-4000 live births. Detected on newborn bloodspot screening (elevated TSH).

Most common cause is thyroid dysgenesis (~85%) — agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopic tissue.

Levothyroxine should start as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, ideally within the first 2 weeks of life. Early treatment allows essentially normal cognitive development.

cards.front: Salbutamol relaxes airway smooth muscle by raising intracellular [___], which lowers intracellular calcium.
cards.context:
Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist. The receptor is a Gs-coupled GPCR on airway smooth muscle, so agonism raises cyclic AMP, activates protein kinase A, and lowers intracellular calcium.

Lower calcium means the smooth muscle relaxes and the airway opens. That is a purely mechanical effect on calibre.

The crucial corollary is that nothing in this pathway touches the airway inflammation. That is why relief is fast and why it wears off.

cards.front: A child with slapped cheek disease is no longer [___] once the facial rash appears, so exclusion from school achieves nothing.
cards.context:
THE TIMING INVERTS THE OBVIOUS ADVICE. A child with parvovirus B19 is infectious during the earlier viraemic, coryzal phase — and is NO LONGER INFECTIOUS by the time the slapped cheek rash appears.

So excluding the child from school once you can see the rash achieves nothing: the transmission has already happened, to people who had no idea anyone was ill. They do not need to be kept home for the rash.

This is worth holding precisely because it is backwards from every other exanthem instinct, where a visible rash means keep them away from others.

cards.front: Pneumococcus, group A streptococcus and [___] are common causes of childhood empyema.
cards.context:
Empyema is an infected pleural collection complicating pneumonia. Persistent fever or deterioration despite treatment should prompt reassessment.

Antibiotic choice follows the local pathway and cultures; ultrasound helps define the collection and guide drainage planning.

cards.front: Anaemia is first sorted by red-cell size (MCV): a low MCV is microcytic, and the commonest paediatric cause of that picture is [___].
cards.context:
MCV (mean corpuscular volume) is the cell-size dimension and the first branch of the work-up. Low MCV = small cells = microcytic; high = macrocytic; in-range = normocytic.

The three commonest microcytic causes are iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, and (rarely in children) anaemia of chronic disease.

cards.front: After immediate urticaria following peanut ingestion, first-line testing for IgE-mediated allergy is [___] prick.
cards.context:
IgE-mediated food allergy presents within minutes to 2 hours with urticaria, angioedema, or anaphylaxis.

Skin prick testing detects sensitisation in vivo; a positive result still requires a convincing exposure history to confirm clinical allergy.

cards.front: First-line treatment for atopic dermatitis is [___] combined with regular emollients.
cards.context:
Atopic eczema is a combined barrier defect (filaggrin LOF) + Th2-skewed immune response.

Parents need: use enough steroid (a fingertip unit covers two adult palm areas), twice daily for 1-2 weeks of a flare, then taper rather than stopping abruptly, and continue emollients on clear skin.
